note.note:
Consult Summary:
- 25–40-year-old woman (age not specified) with 2 days of gradual, worsening suprapubic burning abdominal pain, mild nausea, subjective feverishness and pink-discolored urine; clinician suspected acute lower urinary tract infection and empirically prescribed antibiotics while arranging/ recommending urine and pregnancy testing and follow-up.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Lower central abdominal (suprapubic, just below the umbilicus) burning pain for ~2 days; constant and gradually worsening; sore to pressure.
  - Subjective hot/sweaty feeling; mild nausea; no vomiting.
  - Noticed pink-coloured urine and increased urinary frequency (patient attributes frequency partly to increased fluid intake); denies stinging or clear dysuria.
- Timeline:
  - Symptoms began ~2 days ago, gradual onset, progressively worse but patient still ambulatory and functioning.
  - Recent constipation last week that has since improved; current bowel movements reported normal.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Pain worse with pressure; no clear relieving factors noted.
- Associated symptoms / systems review:
  - No vomiting, no cough, no dyspnea, no palpitations, no headache, no vision changes.
  - Gynecologic: sexually active with one partner; Implanon implant placed ~1 year ago; last sexual activity 4 days ago; last period ~2 weeks ago; last STI screen normal ~6 months ago.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No vomiting, no objective fever recorded, no flank pain, no vaginal bleeding explicitly reported, no abnormal vaginal discharge reported.

Past Medical History:
- Generally fit and well by report.
- No prior surgeries.
- Contraception: Implanon implant inserted ~1 year ago.

Medications:
- Implanon implant — dose/route/frequency not documented (implant noted).
- Trimethoprim — prescribed empirically for suspected urinary tract infection; transcript instruction included both the phrases "two tablets" and "one tablet twice a day for three days" (ambiguous/conflict noted regarding dose); route not explicitly stated.
- Paracetamol advised for pain relief — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- No other regular medications reported.
Allergies:
- Not documented.

Social History:
- Lives in a share house with two roommates.
- Occupation: accountant; currently working.
- Smoking: denies.
- Alcohol: social use; no excess reported.
- No recreational drug use documented.

Family History:
- No relevant family history reported.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Not recorded by clinician.
- Patient reports localized suprapubic tenderness when pressing the area.

Investigations:
- No lab or imaging results documented.
- Tests discussed / to be arranged (per clinician): urine testing (urinalysis / MSU) and pregnancy test; clinician discussed organizing tests today but results not present in record.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
- Working diagnosis: Suspected acute lower urinary tract infection (cystitis) — clinician treated empirically with antibiotics and arranged/ recommended testing (urine and pregnancy test).

DDx Integration (brief):
- 1) Acute lower urinary tract infection (cystitis) — supporting: suprapubic burning pain, suprapubic tenderness to pressure, increased urinary frequency, pink urine; opposing: patient denies dysuria and no objective fever recorded. (Aligned with transcript and DDx; clinician empirically treated.)
- 2) Urolithiasis (ureteric/bladder stone) — supporting: hematuria-compatible pink urine, lower abdominal pain, nausea; opposing: pain described as constant burning rather than classic colicky flank-to-groin pain and no reported severe radiating pain. (Consistent with DDx as alternative.)
- 3) Gynecologic causes (ectopic pregnancy, ovarian cyst rupture/torsion) — supporting: lower pelvic pain, possible bleeding; opposing: Implanon in place (lowers pregnancy risk), no clear vaginal bleeding described, and no acute hemodynamic instability. (Consistent with DDx; pregnancy to be ruled out.)

Issue 1: Suspected acute lower urinary tract infection (cystitis)
- Assessment:
  - Clinical presentation most consistent with lower UTI (suprapubic burning pain, urinary frequency, discolored urine, mild systemic symptoms).
- Plan:
  - Start empiric antibiotic therapy: Trimethoprim prescribed by clinician; transcript contains ambiguous dosing language ("two tablets" and also "one tablet twice a day for three days") — dosing/route/frequency unclear (conflict/ambiguous wording documented).
  - Recommend urine testing (urinalysis and/or midstream urine culture) to confirm infection and guide therapy — to be organized/collected.
  - Analgesia: regular paracetamol as needed (dose not documented).
  - Hydration and supportive measures; cranberry juice suggested as an adjunct for urinary symptoms.
  - Safety-netting: return or seek urgent care if worsening abdominal pain, persistent or high fever, vomiting, increasing systemic symptoms or no improvement within a few days.
  - Follow-up: clinician advised to re-evaluate in a few days if not improving.

Issue 2: Possible urolithiasis (urinary tract stone)
- Assessment:
  - Considered given pink urine (possible hematuria) and lower abdominal pain; pain description less typical for ureteric colic.
- Plan:
  - Perform/obtain urinalysis for hematuria (already discussed as part of urine testing).
  - If significant hematuria, severe or colicky pain, or no improvement, consider imaging (e.g., renal tract ultrasound or CT) and urology referral as indicated (to be arranged if clinically warranted).

Issue 3: Gynecologic causes including pregnancy-related complications (ectopic pregnancy) or ovarian pathology
- Assessment:
  - Ectopic pregnancy and ovarian pathology included in differential given lower pelvic pain and possible bleeding; Implanon reduces but does not eliminate pregnancy risk.
- Plan:
  - Obtain a pregnancy test (recommended by clinician) to exclude pregnancy/ectopic pregnancy.
  - If pregnancy positive, or if pain persists/worsens or new vaginal bleeding/signs of peritonitis develop, arrange urgent gynecologic assessment and pelvic ultrasound.
  - Consider pelvic exam and STI testing if clinically indicated (not documented as completed during this visit).

General plan items:
- Explain plan and safety-netting to patient; patient agreed.
- Prescription to be sent to pharmacy for collection.
- Arrange/perform urine test and pregnancy test promptly; review results and modify treatment accordingly.
- Return for review if symptoms worsen or fail to improve within a few days.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs not recorded; urine test and pregnancy test results not documented; allergies list not documented (no allergies stated).
- Conflicts/ambiguities:
  - Medication dosing ambiguity for Trimethoprim in transcript ("two tablets" vs "one tablet twice a day for three days") — conflict/unclear dosing documented.
  - No direct conflict between transcript and DDx; DDx supports clinician’s working diagnosis.
- Transcript quality: overall clear; one ambiguous phrase regarding antibiotic dosing as noted above.
